tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

type.description: What kind of feedback this is.

title.description: Short, specific one-line summary of the issue.

details.description: Labeled bullets, in order: **What happened:** (observed vs. expected, exact error text if short); **What the user said:** (quoted, or "User didn't comment; observed by the model."); **Repro:** (minimal steps); **Evidence:** (request IDs, timestamps, paths, versions; omit if none); optionally a final **Cause:** only if verified in-session. One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

task_category.description: What kind of task the session was doing when the issue occurred, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

FEVO is a New York-based social commerce company that sells sports and live-event tickets through group-buying tools.

- **Clients:** It works with more than 700 brands in North American sports and live events. Existing clients include the New York Yankees, Miami Dolphins, New York Giants, Los Angeles Dodgers and Milwaukee Bucks. Its 2022 NASCAR deal designated FEVO as a "Social Ticketing Partner of NASCAR."

**Caveats:**
- A jobs-aggregator page states that founder Ari Daie and CFO Himanshu Kothari departed abruptly in September 2024. I found no corroborating source, so verify it before relying on it.
- Don't confuse FEVO with **Fever**, a separate discovery and ticketing platform. Fever has recent sports deals, such as taking over Bristol Sport's ticketing from SeatGeek and being LIV Golf's official global ticketing partner.

The Level III/secondary enforcement group reviews and processes those reports.
- Member institutions and conferences also use RSRO to submit interpretation requests to the NCAA's Governance and Member Services staff. All other interpretive requests should be submitted via RSRO. - LSDBi is a separate, web-based NCAA database. It launched in August 2000 and was established to house updated division manuals and more than 9,000 interpretations of NCAA rules.

- Per a 2006 NCAA News article, LSDBi also features infractions databases, and provides assistance in submitting waiver requests. A 2002 article said members could search and retrieve legislative proposals, major and secondary infractions cases, and student-athlete reinstatement cases.

The name combines TMG with "BioMedical Consulting," per its in-house developed muscle diagnostics methodology, Tensiomyography, and the other half, "BioMedical Consulting".

**The devices:** The TMG S2 is described as a patented tensiomyography measuring device developed with the Laboratory for Biomedical and Muscle Biomechanics at the University of Ljubljana. Other models named in the results are the TMG100 and TMG PRO. One study describes the TMG S2 as the device used for its measurements (the TMG S2 device (TMG Measurement System, TMG-BMC Ltd., Ljubljana, Slovenia)). The company also sells MC sensors for cycling and other applications.

**How it works:** The TMG sensor measures muscle radial displacement during twitch contractions induced by short electrical stimuli. The electrodes go on the skin, and the sensor is positioned perpendicularly to the tangential plane on the largest area above the muscle belly.

**Common parameters:** Studies typically report delay time (Td), contraction time (Tc), sustain time (Ts), and relaxation time (Tr). For example, time of contraction (Tc) represented the time between 10% and 90% of the maximum vertical muscle movement.

**Caveat:** Most of these sources are from TMG-BMC's own website or partner pages. Claims such as TMG is the standard for accurate, non-invasive and cost-effective muscle performance assessment are marketing language, not independent findings. For independent evidence, look at peer-reviewed studies that use the device.

Links: [{"title":"compliance assistant","url":"https://www.ncaa.org/what-we-do/programs/compliance-assistant/"},{"title":"compliance assistant","url":"https://www.ncaa.org/compliance-assistant"},{"title":"www.ncaa.org","url":"https://www.ncaa.org/?p=7181"},{"title":"compliance assistant","url":"https://www.ncaa.org/sports/2013/11/19/compliance-assistant.aspx"},{"title":"Compliance Assistant","url":"https://careers.insidehighered.com/job/1883781/compliance-assistant/"},{"title":"041509 AFI1b Review of NCAA Eligibility Compliance Audit","url":"https://www.fau.edu/bot/files/April_2009/041509_AFI1b_Review_of_NCAA_Eligibility_Compliance_Audit.pdf"},{"title":"NCAA Compliance Assistant (Administrative Assistant 1)","url":"https://www.academicjobs.com/university-jobs/ncaa-compliance-assistant-administrative-assistant-1/710360"},{"title":"Posted Date: Oct 25, 2024","url":"https://intercollegiate.co/job/ncaa-compliance-assistant-104991"},{"title":"National Collegiate Athletic Association","url":"https://s3.amazonaws.com/ncaanewsarchive/1999/19990719/active/3615n10.html"}]

The official NCAA page describes Compliance Assistant as a tool that helps athletic departments and student-athletes stay in line with NCAA legislation. It covers financial aid, eligibility, recruiting, athletics personnel, and playing and practice seasons, and it doubles as a data-collection system for generating NCAA-required forms. The program, its documentation, and technical support are free to NCAA membership.

Access is handled by single-source sign-on administrators at each member school or conference, and users open it through My Apps. Questions can go to complianceassistant@ncaa.org.

A few sources add context on CAi, though none is an official NCAA description of it. A 2009 university audit report calls it the NCAA Compliance Assistant - Internet (CAi) database, which is designed to assist institutions in creating and maintaining compliance records, and monitoring student-athlete eligibility. A newer NCAA page refers users to a Compliance Assistant 2.0 app's resource section for user guides and webinars, which suggests the current version is 2.0.

The search didn't turn up any product called "Donation Exchange." The results were mostly college athletics donation-request policies, which suggests colleges handle these requests through their own forms and compliance review rather than a named third-party app.

- **Online request systems:** Texas Tech says all athletic department donation requests must be submitted through the online donation request system and must be received at least six (6) weeks prior to the date your item is needed.
- **Compliance review:** UCLA says all donation requests are subject to review by UCLA Athletics for NCAA compliance purposes.
- **Paperwork:** Boston College requires a request form and a letter on the organization's letterhead, and donation requests will NOT be approved without the completed request form AND an official letter from the organization.
- **Prohibited recipients:** Liberty's policy notes that NCAA Bylaw 13.15 prohibits institutional staff members from participating in donating memorabilia to any organization, event, or activity that involves or benefits prospect-aged individuals (9th – 12th grade and junior college students).

VCU's compliance page lists something called "VCU Exchange" under its NIL section, but the result doesn't describe it as a donor or donation app, so I can't tie it to your query. If you're looking for a specific vendor, a search with the college's name plus "donation request portal" would likely be more productive.

Compliance Assistant - NCAA.org - The Official Website of the NCAA
The Compliance Assistant program is a tool designed to help administrators ensure that their athletic department and student-athletes are in compliance with NCAA legislation. In addition to applying NCAA legislation in the areas of financial aid, eligibility, recruiting, athletics personnel and playing and practice seasons, it is a data-collection system that can be used to generate NCAA-required forms and other forms created by the user. This program, documentation and technical support are pro
Access to the Compliance Assistant (CA) application is managed by single-source sign-on (SSO) administrators at each NCAA member school and conference.
Authorized users may access CA by clicking the My Apps link at the top of the page. If Compliance Assistant does not appear in My Apps, contact your SSO administrator.
For user guides, upcoming and recorded webinars and additional resources, please visit the Compliance Assistant 2.0 app’s resource section.

With Equipment Manager™, coaches, administrators and equipment managers have instant access to the history of their equipment so that old equipment can be systematically purged from inventory.

The Compliance Assistant program is a tool designed to help administrators ensure that their athletic department and student-athletes are in compliance with NCAA legislation.
